blocks.text: “You see, I do not know how to find any particular part of the diary.” Even while he was speaking, an idea came to him. He spoke in a different voice, simply and without thinking, like an innocent child: “That’s quite true, I promise you. Honest Indian!” I could not help smiling, and he made a face. “I let the truth slip out that time!” he said. “I have kept the diary for months now. But do you know, I never once thought about how I would find a particular part of it? I never thought about it in case I wanted to look something up.” By this time I had made up my mind. Dr. Seward was a doctor who had looked after Lucy. So his diary might add something to what we already knew about that terrible Being. I said boldly:—
“Then, Dr. Seward, you had better let me copy it out for you on my typewriter.” His face became as pale as death as he said:—
“No! no! no! I wouldn’t let you know that terrible story for anything in the world!”

So it was terrible; my feeling about it was right! For a moment I thought. My eyes moved around the room. Without really meaning to, I was looking for something to help me, or some chance to use. Then my eyes stopped on a big pile of typed pages on the table. He saw the look in my eyes. Without thinking, he looked where I was looking. When he saw the pile of papers, he understood what I meant.

“You do not know me,” I said. “I have typed my own diary and my husband’s diary too. When you have read those papers, you will know me better. I have not held back in this cause. I have given it every thought of my own heart. But, of course, you do not know me—yet. So I must not expect you to trust me that much.”

He is certainly a man of very fine and good character; poor dear Lucy was right about him. He stood up and opened a large drawer. Inside it, in neat order, were a number of hollow metal tubes covered with dark wax. He said:—

“You are quite right. I did not trust you because I did not know you. But I know you now. And let me say that I should have known you long ago. I know that Lucy told you about me; she told me about you too. I want to make up for my mistake, and there is only one way I can do it. May I? Take the cylinders and listen to them. The first six are about my own private life, and they will not fill you with horror. Then you will know me better. By then dinner will be ready. Meanwhile, I shall read some of these papers. Then I shall understand certain things better.” He carried the phonograph up to my sitting-room himself and set it up for me. Now I shall learn something pleasant, I am sure. It will tell me the other side of a true love story. I already know one side of it....

29 September.—I was so deep in that wonderful diary of Jonathan Harker, and in his wife’s diary too, that I lost track of the time. The maid came to say that dinner was ready, but Mrs. Harker had not come down. So I said: “Perhaps she is tired; let dinner wait an hour.” Then I went on with my work. I had just finished Mrs. Harker’s diary when she came in. She looked sweet and pretty, but very sad, and her eyes were red from crying. For some reason this moved me very much. God knows, I have had reasons to cry lately! But I could not find the relief that tears bring. And now I saw those sweet eyes, bright from her recent tears, and the sight went straight to my heart. So I said as gently as I could:—
“I am very much afraid that I have upset you.”

“Oh, no, you have not upset me,” she replied, “but your sadness has moved me more than I can say. That is a wonderful machine, but it is cruelly true. I could hear the terrible pain in your heart in the very sound of your voice. It was like a soul crying out to Almighty God. No one must ever hear those words spoken again! Look, I have tried to be useful. I have copied out the words on my typewriter. Now nobody else needs to hear your heart beat, as I did.”
